title: 10 Interactive Ideas for Virtual Mental Health Groups
summary: Group gone quiet? Ten activities you can run in your next online session, what each one is for, and what to do if one falls flat.
body_markdown:
Ten activities you can use in your next online session. Each one includes what it is for, how to set it up, and what to do when it does not land, because some of them will not, and that is normal.


They are ordered roughly from lowest to highest commitment. If your group is new or quiet, start at the top. If they already know each other, the later ones will do more for you.


## Why engagement is harder online


A room does a lot of work for you that a video call does not. In person, people arrive early and talk in the doorway. They read each other's posture. Silence feels shared rather than broken.


Online, none of that happens by itself. A group can be well run and still feel flat, and members drift, not because they stopped needing the group, but because nothing pulled them back in. The activities below are ways of doing on purpose what a physical room does by accident.


None of this is treatment. These are psychoeducational activities for expert-led support groups: they build connection, shared language and participation. They are not a substitute for care, and they are not designed to process trauma in the moment.


## 1. Two Truths and a Lie, wellness edition


**Time** 10–15 minutes · **Best for** A group in its first three or four sessions


### How to run it


Each member shares two true statements and one false one about their own wellbeing or their week. The group guesses which is the lie.


*Example:* Ask for statements about the last week rather than about their history: 'I went for a walk every day', 'I cooked something new', 'I called my sister'.


### Why it works


It gives people a structured way to disclose something real while keeping full control of how much they reveal. The guessing takes the weight out of it.


### Getting it right


Set one rule before you start: nothing you would not want repeated outside this room. It sounds obvious, and saying it out loud is what makes people relax. Cap it at four or five people per session rather than going round everybody. A long circuit turns a warm-up into an ordeal, and the members at the end spend the whole time rehearsing instead of listening.


### When it does not land


If the group goes quiet, the prompt was too personal. Move it to something lighter: three statements about your week, not your history. And go first yourself, with a mild example, so the ceiling is visible.


## 2. Would You Rather, wellness edition


**Time** 10 minutes · **Best for** A quiet group, or the first ten minutes of any session


### How to run it


Pose paired choices about self-care and habits: journal for ten minutes or walk for thirty, meditate in the morning or write a gratitude list. Members vote, then say why.


*Example:* 'Would you rather cancel on a friend and feel guilty, or go when you have nothing left?' A real dilemma gets further than a lifestyle preference.


### Why it works


Voting is a zero-risk first action. People who will not speak unprompted will click a button, and the 'why' conversation usually opens up from there.


### Getting it right


Use whatever polling tool your platform already has rather than introducing new software; a show of hands works fine. The value is not in the vote, it is in the follow-up question, so always ask two or three people why they chose what they chose. If the room is warm enough, ask whether anyone changed their mind while listening.


### When it does not land


Often the questions are too abstract. Make them concrete and slightly uncomfortable. 'Would you rather cancel on a friend or go when you have no energy' gets a real conversation where 'meditate or journal' does not.


## 3. The kindness thread


**Time** Ongoing, a few minutes a week · **Best for** Any group that meets less often than weekly


### How to run it


Keep a running channel or shared document where members post appreciation for each other between sessions. Give it a rhythm. One day a week works better than 'whenever'.


*Example:* 'Thank you to whoever said the thing about not having to be fine. I thought about it all week.'


### Why it works


It keeps the group alive in the six days nobody is in a meeting, which is where most groups quietly lose people.


### Getting it right


Give it a name and a day. 'Thursday thank-yous' gets used; 'the appreciation channel' does not. Keep a light hand on moderation but do step in if it turns into advice-giving, which is the most common way these threads go wrong. If your group meets on a platform without a persistent space, a shared document works and is easier for members who dislike another app.


### When it does not land


Threads die without a host. Seed it yourself for the first three weeks, name specific people, and let anonymous submissions in for members who find public praise uncomfortable.


## 4. The gratitude jar, digital version


**Time** One minute to add, 10 minutes to read back · **Best for** Groups running eight weeks or longer


### How to run it


Each member adds one small win or moment of gratitude, as often as they like. At the end of the month, read a selection back to the group.


*Example:* 'Got out of bed before nine.' 'The bus came straight away.' 'My kid laughed at my joke.'


### Why it works


The reading-back is the part that matters. Seeing a month of small things collected together shows a group its own progress, which individuals rarely notice in themselves.


### Getting it right


Say explicitly that small entries are the point, because people arrive assuming they need something impressive. Read back a selection rather than everything, and read them anonymously unless someone has asked to be named. The read-back lands hardest at the end of a month or a cycle, when a group is most likely to feel it has not moved.


### When it does not land


If contributions dry up, the bar is too high. 'One good thing' beats 'what are you grateful for'. And drop the daily expectation before you drop the activity.


## 5. Member-led skill or interest share


**Time** 10 minutes per member · **Best for** Groups past the two-month mark


### How to run it


One member shows the group something they are good at or care about: cooking, a craft, music, a hobby. Ten minutes, live or pre-recorded.


*Example:* Someone walking the group through how they make bread, or reading two minutes of something they wrote.


### Why it works


Groups can accidentally define members by their hardest thing. This is the clearest way to interrupt that, and people behave differently toward each other afterward.


### Getting it right


Ask privately and specifically: 'you mentioned you garden. Would you show us something for ten minutes in two weeks?' An open call to the room tends to produce silence. Schedule one per session rather than a showcase; a whole session of performances is a lot of pressure and it crowds out the ordinary conversation the group came for.


### When it does not land


Nobody volunteers first. Ask one person privately and in advance rather than opening it to the room, and make the first one deliberately modest so the bar stays low.


## 6. Five minutes of shared quiet


**Time** 5 minutes · **Best for** Every group, at the start or the end


### How to run it


Open or close with a short breathing or grounding exercise. Rotate who leads it once the group is comfortable.


*Example:* Sixty seconds of noticing sound, then three slow breaths, then naming one thing you want from the next hour.


### Why it works


It marks the session as different from the rest of the day, and it gives latecomers a soft landing. Rotating the lead also builds the confidence of members who might run a group themselves one day.


### Getting it right


Keep it short and keep it the same each week. The familiarity is what makes it work. Avoid anything that asks people to close their eyes and revisit a memory; that is a different kind of exercise and it belongs with a clinician, not in a psychoeducational group. If someone opts out visibly every week, leave it alone and do not check in about it publicly.


### When it does not land


Some people find guided exercises uncomfortable and will not say so. Offer it as optional from the start, keep cameras-off acceptable, and never comment on who joined in.


## 7. A collaborative puzzle or challenge


**Time** 15–20 minutes · **Best for** A group that has gone polite and needs to do something together


### How to run it


Set a problem the group solves together: a themed quiz, a set of clues, anything with one shared goal and no individual winner.


*Example:* A set of clues that can only be solved by pooling what different people know.


### Why it works


It moves people from talking about themselves to working alongside each other, which is a different and sometimes easier kind of closeness.


### Getting it right


Design it so no single person can finish it alone, and make sure at least one part rewards a kind of knowledge that is not academic. Skip anything timed if the group includes people managing anxiety. If it stalls, join in as a participant rather than a host. A facilitator solving it for them is worse than an unfinished puzzle.


### When it does not land


Competitive framing backfires fast in a support group. If it gets tense, drop the timer and the scoring and let it become a conversation.


## 8. A group read


**Time** One session · **Best for** Groups with a settled core of regulars


### How to run it


Pick one book or one essay and give it a session. Short pieces work better than books for most groups.


*Example:* A single essay or a chapter, sent out a week ahead, with two questions attached.


### Why it works


It gives people something outside themselves to talk through, which is often how they end up saying the thing they could not say directly.


### Getting it right


Choose short. An essay gets read; a book gets bought and not read, and then people skip the session out of embarrassment. Send two questions with it so members who did read have somewhere to start. Summarize it in five minutes at the top so the ones who did not read are never exposed. That summary is not a concession, it is what makes the session work.


### When it does not land


Half the group will not have read it. Plan for that: summarize it in five minutes at the start so nobody has to admit it, and choose shorter pieces next time.


## 9. A seven-day group challenge


**Time** A few minutes a day for a week · **Best for** Groups that want momentum between sessions


### How to run it


One simple daily action for a week, tracked somewhere everyone can see. Keep the task small enough that a bad day does not break it.


*Example:* 'Step outside once a day.' Not 'exercise daily'.


### Why it works


Accountability between sessions, and a shared reference point when you next meet.


### Getting it right


Pick something achievable on the worst day of somebody's week, because that is the day that decides whether the challenge survives. Track the group total rather than individual streaks. When you review it, ask what got in the way rather than who completed it. The obstacles are the useful conversation and the completion rate is not.


### When it does not land


Public tracking shames the people who miss days. Make it opt-in, celebrate the group total rather than individuals, and never name who dropped off.


## 10. Recognition that is not a leaderboard


**Time** Two minutes a session · **Best for** Every group, permanently


### How to run it


Notice contribution out loud. A brief thank-you, a member spotlight in a newsletter, a note to someone who supported another member well.


*Example:* 'I noticed you stayed behind to talk to someone last week. That mattered.'


### Why it works


People stay where they feel seen. This is the cheapest retention tool a facilitator has.


### Getting it right


Specific beats general: name the thing they did, not the quality you are ascribing to them. Spread it around deliberately and keep a private note of who you have not mentioned lately, because it is easy to over-notice the confident members. Avoid anything cumulative (badges, counts, levels) because the moment recognition can be ranked, the quieter half of the room reads it as a scoreboard they are losing.


### When it does not land


If it starts to feel like a performance metric, stop. Recognition should never make quieter members feel they are failing at the group.


## Choosing which one to use


You do not need ten activities. Most groups run well on two or three that suit them, used consistently, plus one low-commitment thing that keeps the group present between sessions.


If you only take one thing from this: pick the activity that matches how well your group already knows each other, not the one that sounds best. A group in week two and a group in month eight need different things, and the most common facilitation mistake is running an intimate exercise before the room can hold it.


## Questions leaders ask


### How many activities should one session include?


One. Two at most, and only if one of them is a short opener. A session that runs three activities stops being a support group and starts being a workshop, and the conversation that people actually came for gets squeezed out. The activity is there to open the room, not to fill it.


### What if members refuse to take part?


Let them. Participation that has been extracted is worth very little, and a member who sits out one week will often join in the next once they have seen how it goes. What does damage is drawing attention to it: naming someone who has not spoken, or asking them directly in front of everyone. Make opting out visibly normal and it stops being a statement.


### Do these work for a group that meets in person?


Most of them, yes. The between-session ones (the kindness thread, the gratitude collection, the seven-day challenge) were designed around the problem that an online group disappears completely between meetings, so they earn less in a room where people already chat before and after. The in-session activities transfer directly.


### How long before a new group is ready for the more personal activities?


There is no fixed number, but a useful signal is whether anyone has disagreed with anyone yet. A group that is still entirely agreeable is usually still being polite, and polite groups are not ready to be vulnerable. The first four activities on this list suit that stage; the member-led share and the group read work better once the politeness has worn off.
